paragraphs.text:
By the same Gregory of Nyssa: On what "in the image of God and in his likeness" means.

Those who wish to see accurately the God-created beauty of their own face can reflect their own image and the features of their face in no other way than by means of a perfectly clear mirror. When they bring the image of their own appearance close to it, they see plainly within it, and through it, a kind of counterpart, an impression in their own image and likeness. Let us too, then, gaze as into a mirror toward the divine ray of the spiritual sun, and from there learn clearly the reflection, the form and the image of what in our nature is "in the image and likeness." For the making of man is, it truly is, as it seems to me, something awesome and hard to explain, portraying in itself many hidden mysteries of God. And just as the eye easily perceives things outside itself but cannot perceive what it is itself, so the principle of our creation has proved hard to see and hard to grasp for every eye of human understanding. For when the Creator had completed the simple and wholly spiritual world of the invisible powers, and after it this material and visible world composed of four elements, he then says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." And he makes a living being, like a kind of mixed world akin to both worlds, composed of an incorporeal, immortal and incorruptible soul and of a material, visible body made of four elements. When man had come into being, Scripture says again, "And God made man; in the image of God he made him"; and by "God" it means the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Many different opinions on this have been put forward by the interpreters. Some said that what is "in the image and likeness of God" is man's power to rule and exercise authority; others, the spiritual and invisible nature of the soul; others, the incorruption and sinlessness of the time when

Adam came into being; and still others have said that it is a prophecy about baptism. Last of all, as to one untimely born, it has fallen to me too to say a few things about this. And first of all it is worth asking this: why did God not rather call the spiritual, immaterial and heavenly angels, who are near to God, "in his image and likeness"? For they too have the power to rule and exercise authority over the whole earth and over man himself, or rather a power above man's. Likewise incorruption, immateriality, invisibility, purity, and every other praise you might speak of Adam are present in surpassing measure in the spiritual and heavenly choirs of the bodiless beings. So "in the image" hints at something in man deeper than the views just set out. For man possesses not just one image and likeness of God, but also a second and a third. As in a mirror, and in a sketch that is typological rather than natural, he portrays the mystery of the Godhead in three hypostases; and not only that, but he also clearly foreshadows the incarnation of God the Word, one of the Holy Trinity. And perhaps the soul by itself is "in the image" of the Godhead, while the composite of our soul and body is "in the likeness" of the Word's taking flesh. But let us rather run back to the very beginning of the discussion, and from there, as from a very deep spring, first ask this: why did God not make our forefathers and chief hypostases, I mean Adam, Eve and the son who came forth from them, in the manner of the other rational beings, that is, the angels, or again on the same footing as the animals? Instead, he brought Adam into existence without a cause and unbegotten, and the second man after him, his son, begotten. Eve, however, was neither begotten nor yet uncaused, but taken, that is, proceeding: she came forth from the substance of the uncaused Adam, ineffably given her own substance [?]. Might it not be, then, that these three heads of all humanity, the first-born, consubstantial hypostases, came into being typologically after a kind of image of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, as Methodius thinks? The uncaused and unbegotten Adam has the type and image of the uncaused almighty God and Father, the cause of all things; his begotten son foreshadows the image of the begotten Son and Word of God; and Eve, who proceeded, signifies the proceeding hypostasis of the Holy Spirit. That is why God did not breathe the breath of life into her: because she was a type of the breath and life of the Holy Spirit, and because she was to receive, through the Holy Spirit, God, who truly is the breath and life of all things. Hence one may see and marvel that the unbegotten Adam had no other unbegotten and uncaused being like himself among men, and neither did Eve who proceeded, since they are true types of the unbegotten Father and of the Holy Spirit. But the begotten son had all men, who are begotten sons, as brothers

like himself, since he exists in the typological image and likeness of Christ the begotten Son, who became man, the firstborn without seed among many brothers. If it is not so, and "in the image" does not mean this, why were there not four, or two, or more hypostases of the forefathers, with varying hypostatic properties (I mean unbegottenness, begottenness and procession), but three and three only? So you have, in typological image and likeness, a trinity in a unity, in three hypostases. It follows that you should next learn the unity in the trinity as well. How you may rightly discern this, listen to one of the wise who exhorts you and says: "If you wish to know God, first know yourself": from your own composition, he says, from your own constitution, from what is [?] within yourself. Go in, sink down into yourself, look closely as in a mirror into your own soul, examine its constitution, and you will see that you are in the image and likeness of God. The spiritual and immortal substance of your soul is nameless and unknown, in the typological image of the nameless, unknowable and immortal God. For no human being who has ever lived has known the substance either of God or of the rational soul. The soul gives life to the body's four-element nature, holds it together and provides for it, in the image of God, who provides for the whole four-cornered creation and for the creation above. So we do not know the place where God dwells, but only believe that he is everywhere; nor do we know the place in the body where the soul dwells, but only know that it is present and active in the whole body. Your soul also has another thing in the image of God: I mean that it is of a different substance from all created nature. But the most paradoxical feature of the image within us is this: the human mind can grasp neither the principles of God's existence nor the substance of our soul, how it naturally comes into existence and arrives. Hence those who formed wrong doctrines in trying to grasp this have stumbled in these ways. Some say that souls are sent down from heaven into bodies; others say that they come into existence together with the body, created by God; others say that man, being in the image of the Creator, generates the soul too, along with the seed; others say that the soul is produced from both parties, male and female, as when a stone and iron strike together and produce fire by the heat. And some say that the soul too comes into being at the very instant of the conception of the [?]; others say on the fortieth

day after conception, adducing what they take to be proof of this from the Law. And some imagined the soul to be of the same substance as the angels; others, that it is below; others, in the air; others, that it exists throughout the universe as a kind of divine substance. That is why, though it is united to a body and, being in the image of God, gives that body life, it remains untouched by the bodily passions and the corruptions of the body. It is neither seen nor explained nor grasped in its nature, nor in form, shape, outline, quality, quantity, existence, composition or beauty. Hence Methodius too says in the Symposium that the soul has an inconceivable and indescribable beauty, and that for this reason it is, as it were, envied and lusted after by the hostile spirits, since it is clothed with a form superior to those spiritual beings themselves. All the incomprehensibility, obscurity and uncertainty that surround the soul hint at nothing other than that it is properly and truly the image of the incomprehensible God. So, though we are ignorant of everything about it, we are assured of its existence only from its activities in the body, just as we confirm the existence of God from his works in the visible creation.

But now let us come to the most crucial point of "in the image and likeness," so as to show, as promised, the unity of the Godhead in Trinity. What is this? Clearly, once again, our soul, and its rational word, and the mind, which the Apostle called spirit when he commands us to be holy in soul, body and spirit. For the soul, again, is unbegotten and uncaused, as a type of the unbegotten and uncaused God and Father. Its rational word is not unbegotten, but is begotten from it ineffably, invisibly, inexplicably and without passion. The mind is neither uncaused nor unbegotten, but proceeds, running through everything, surveying all things and feeling its way invisibly, in the image and likeness of the all-holy and proceeding Spirit, of whom it is said, "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." The soul does not proceed as long as it is in the body, since if it did, we would be dying every hour. Our word is not unbegotten, since otherwise we would be irrational, like beasts. But the most paradoxical of these paradoxes is this: we have a simple soul, and likewise a single, uncompounded mind, but a word that is twofold in its birth while remaining one and undivided. For the word is begotten in the heart by an incomprehensible and incorporeal birth, and remains within, unknown; and it is born by a second, bodily birth through the lips, and then becomes known to all. Yet it is not separated from the soul that begot it. So through the two births of our word we may clearly learn, by image and likeness, the two births of God the Word.

For he was begotten invisibly, inexplicably and incomprehensibly from the Father before the ages. And he was unknown, as though within a soul, with the Father, until he was born according to the flesh, as from a heart, from the holy Virgin, without corruption and without seed, and appeared to the world, without being separated from the hidden paternal substance of God who begot him. Thus it has been shown that in the unity of our immortal and spiritual soul-substance there are, in image, three hypostatic properties: the unbegottenness of the soul, the begetting of the word, and the procession of the spirit, that is, of the mind. And I take courage and dare to say that it was with this invisible trinitarian view of the soul in mind that the divine Apostle said that man is in the image of the invisible God. If this is not so, why was our soul not made by God [?]-partite or four-partite instead? Why does it have a threefold division, and that only, without confusion, in the image of the holy, consubstantial and life-giving Trinity? So that, if it is permitted to say so, in man too, and above all in the righteous man, the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells, typologically though not naturally, faintly sketching in some way God in Trinity.

Hence the wise men outside the faith also defined our soul as tripartite, though in another way, saying that it has a desiring part, a reasoning part and a spirited part. Through the desiring part it is joined to the love of God; through the reasoning part it receives knowledge and wisdom from him; and through anger it sets itself against the spirits of wickedness. In these three, again, the soul sketches the image of God. For God in Trinity governs and administers three realms in three ways (I mean the heavenly, the earthly and those beneath the earth) by his creative, providential and judging power. Everything that God does, he accomplishes in one of these three ways: by creating, by providing, or by chastening. The image of God's creative power is the soul's desiring part, for desire leads to action; the symbol of his providential power, again, is the soul's reasoning part; and the spirited part is the token of his chastening power. And perhaps desire belongs properly to the soul, for before they can speak at all, infants, as soon as they are alive, at once long for the breast and for sleep. The reasoning part clearly belongs to the word, and the spirited part naturally resides in the mind; that is why one who rages contrary to nature is disturbed in his mind. So if anyone wishes to learn how man is in the image and likeness of God, let him feel his way through these things; let him enter into these and similar inner sanctuaries of thought, and examine the constitution of his own nature, that of the spiritual soul. Let him learn minutely and precisely all its parts, the parts of the parts, the principles, the modes and the processions, the unions, the distinctions, its uniformity, its tripartite nature, its oneness, its duality, its trinity: how it is one and yet contemplated in three, recognized typologically, in the image and likeness of God, as a unity in trinity and a trinity in unity. For that it is one in substance and not one when its own

parts are contemplated, he made [?] clear who said, "I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also; I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also." Or rather, certain people teach us this typological trinity within us, in the image of God, even more clearly. For some reason, often enough, some of them have a soul but lack mind or word; others again are well supplied with soul and word but entirely lacking in mind; others again have mind and soul but are deprived of word. Hence the nature of infants too, born and coming forth as from darkness into light, shows at once that it has the soul, as a type of God the Father, a soul that is potentially spiritual and holds within itself the word and the mind. But as the body gradually advances and grows, it reveals the word second, and that not all at once or suddenly, but first by babbling, as if sketching and foretelling the birth of the Word through flesh. And the presence of the mind becomes evident when the infant advances to full manhood.

"But how," someone says, "do these things bear on the present subject of man?" Very much indeed, my friend. Through them we learn the manner in which God was made manifest and shown forth in the world, as in a body, and how by degrees our nature came to know the mystery of the Trinity. For man was conceived by the seed of the evil one, as in a womb of error, sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death. Then, coming forth into the light of the knowledge of God like an infant at first, he was shown to be alive through the guidance of the Law, recognizing the Father and God as having within himself, as the soul does, the Word and the Spirit, who share his substance. But man could not take in the manifestation of the Word and of the mind, because of great weakness of judgment and his infancy, lest through his very piety he slip into polytheism. Then, as time advanced, our nature in the world grew wise, like a growing infant, taught by God the Father, as though from a soul, to recognize dimly, as through certain indistinct babblings of the prophetic teachings, the trial, the utterance and the appearing of the hidden [?] Word who shares his substance. After these babblings (I mean the Mosaic and prophetic riddles of the word), when the perfect Word of God came forth clearly and articulately, as from lips, from the virginal womb, human nature in the world then came to recognize, along with these and through him, its complete trinitarian fullness, receiving the Holy Spirit as a kind of mind: not one that came to dwell in it by moving in from outside, but from within itself, that is, from the soul

[?] made manifest in it, not as something created [?], nor as brought in from outside, nor as foreign, but substantially, from its own innate and connatural hypostatic existence. [?] The soul brings forth the word that shares its substance and puts forth the spirit of the mind, which is of one nature with it. Though bodiless, it has, like a body, members that are bodiless with it and connatural to it, through which, as through imprints, it is given character, form and composition, although it is above form and shape. It has the spirit of the mind as a kind of bodily breath, and bears the word that lives with it as its life. Deprived of these, the rational and spiritual soul, which is in the image and likeness of God, can neither exist nor be known. So through these things within it we may learn and be taught that neither [?] nor the Son exists before the all-holy Spirit. Rather, just as in the soul there is at once the rational soul, at once with it the word within it, and at once and together within it the spirit that gives life, holds together and completes it, so too there is at once the Father, at once God the Word with the Father, at once the Son with the Father, and together at once the Spirit with the Son and the Father. If you separate the word from the soul and deprive it of the word, your soul is then irrational. Through this image of God you may learn that if you deny God the Word, saying [?] … If you want [to know] the likeness of God, philosophize in this way: come to know the hidden God not from things outside but from those within you; from the trinity within you, recognize the Trinity through realities that truly subsist. For this testimony is surer and more trustworthy than any other from the Law and the Scriptures.

For this reason, and this alone, God fashioned such a living being: because the mystery of the Holy Trinity was going to be proclaimed in the world, hard to explain and incomprehensible as it is. So you have in yourself, in the image and likeness of God, the image and likeness, the types and models, of the Holy Trinity. So, looking at the image in the soul's constitution, you may no longer hesitate over the mystery of the Trinity, nor say any longer, prying into it: "If God is a Trinity, how is he one? And if he is one, as is said, how is he a Trinity? And if the Word is Son, how can an offspring be without beginning along with the one who begot it? And if the Spirit is from the Father, how is it not begotten but proceeding? Which did the Father bring forth first, the Son or the Spirit? And if both at once, are there then brother gods and a twin birth in the Trinity? And how shall we tell the difference between begetting and procession among beings that are bodiless, unmoving and unchanging? And how can the offspring be equal in glory with the one who begot it? And if, then, wishing [?]

[?] the Father, or unwilling. And who is the witness that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are of one substance? And if God the Father is a perfect hypostasis, and the Word of God is a perfect hypostasis, and the Spirit of God is again a perfect hypostasis, what is to stop someone from saying that the mind of God is also another divine hypostasis of God, and the arm another God, and the finger a different hypostasis of God? And likewise the right hand and all the other things that the divine Scripture calls members of God? So that you may not say and reason such things, over which the heretics stumbled and by reasoning so fell, God made you according to the image and likeness of his own triune existence: a kind of figurative trinity, known as a consubstantial unity. If you look at it well, you will find in it, as in a mirror and a figure, everything that is piously proclaimed about God: I mean the threeness of the hypostases, the oneness of the nature, the simultaneity, the indivisibility, the incomprehensibility, the formlessness, the invisibility, the unbegotten, the begotten, the proceeding, the creative, the providential, the judging, the intangible, the incorporeal, the incorruptible, the indestructible, the immortal, the eternal, the inexpressible, the most beautiful. In short, you will find sketched in your soul the figures, the images and the shadows of everything that is piously said of the Godhead. And this is why God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” But the heretics and the unbelievers of today have neither known nor understood these things. For if they had considered rightly what it means for man to be according to the image and likeness, they would not have wavered about the mystery of the Trinity; they would not have subjected what is above nature to natural proofs; they would not have been darkened and said that it is impossible for God to be a Trinity in three hypostases. If Arius had learned what it means to be according to the image, he would not have taught that the Word is of a different substance from the Father. If Macedonius had piously considered what it means to be according to the image, he would not have claimed that the Holy Spirit is a creature. But they were blinded, and suffered the same as those who have the pearl within, in their own bosom, yet do not know it, and wander about searching for it in the deep. See, then, that it is not only in realities that our soul figuratively possesses being in the image of God—figuratively, I say, not as equal in nature. How so? I will make what I mean clear at once. We believe that God the Father is uncircumscribed, and likewise the Son and the Holy Spirit; and therefore, as being unbounded, they also have their proper names mutually implying and bound up with one another. For when one names the Father, it is evident that he has indicated the implication of a Son of his. For how could he be called Father unless a Son were known? Likewise, when one says Spirit, he has signified God, for “God is Spirit,” as Scripture says. Then come from this holy Trinity to its image—I mean the trinity that exists within us—and you will see that its three names too are mutually implying and united.

For when you say a rational and intellectual soul, it is plain that you have signified both word and mind; and when you name word, you have certainly also indicated the rational soul that begets it. Likewise, when you say mind, you have by all means indicated both the soul and the word. For whose mind could it be, if not that of a soul and a word? So, just as they have names that mutually imply and are bound up with one another, so too they have a common and undivided essential activity. For the activity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one and the same: one strength, one power, one will, one purpose. For whatever the Father does, the Son is inseparably his fellow agent; and whatever the Son or the all-holy Spirit accomplishes, the Father works together with them, wholly and indivisibly. For neither does the Son do anything apart from the Father, of himself and by himself, nor does the Father do anything at all without the Son and the Spirit, nor again does the Spirit work anything without the Son and the Father. Come, then, once more from the archetypes to the figure that is according to the image and likeness of God, the figure of our soul, and you will see one and the same activity in us. For neither does the soul accomplish anything without the word, nor the word without the soul, nor again does the mind by itself effect anything apart from the soul and the word, because of their common power and activity, which is of one nature with them, inborn and interlinked, according to the image and likeness of God. And if you tell me that the soul does nothing by itself without the body, we have already said this too: that in this also, being according to the image and likeness, it displays its invisible powers through visible matter. Yet when the soul, pure by nature and in substance, is separated from the body, it is then above all found to be more clear-sighted, simple, untroubled and more luminous, and can more truly be called, and be, according to the image and likeness of God. But if, as is likely, the opponent mocks what has been said, on the ground that we have not shown three properly complete hypostases in the soul on a par with the all-holy Trinity, let the fool learn that the soul is according to the image in a figurative way, and not on a par with the Holy Trinity. Moreover, even in the case of the Godhead it would be a fearful thing to say that the Father has local division and a circumscribed separation from the Son, and the Holy Spirit from him. Do not overlook this either in your likeness to God according to the image: namely, that through the bodily birth of the word from the lips, the virtue and the wisdom, the prudence, the power, the depth and the knowledge of your soul and mind are made known and published to all—this example too showing you that you exist according to the image and likeness of God. For through the birth of God the Word in the flesh, the virtue and the power, the knowledge and the wisdom, and all the other good things of the Father and of the Holy Spirit were made manifest in the world.

1345 [?] For see how many and how great are the achievements of the word in the world, as a figure of God the Word, and how through the word all things are fashioned and hold together. By the word the angels came into being; by the word they honor the Creator; by the word the visible things came to be; by the word creation is enlightened; by the word existing things have been known; by the word alone they have been revealed; by the word the ends of the earth have been shown; by the word we honor the Creator; by the word the knowledge of God has been proclaimed; through the word we have come to know God; through the word all things hold together. And just as a speechless infant is unintelligible to people until the word is born through its lips, so through the birth of God the Word in the flesh all the irrationality of our nature passed away, God the Word having plainly revealed the Father and the Holy Spirit to creation. Hence our soul, as fashioned by God, is not even sent out on service after its release from the body, as the angels are sent. For they are ministering spirits, whereas the souls, above all those of the saints, are lordly spirits according to the image of God. For even if man, after the disobedience, was made a little lower than the angels, yet through the hypostatic union of God the Word in him he has become something greater: for he who was once according to the image of God has now become one with God; and he who formerly partook of the image of God has become one who imparts his own image. To him be the glory to the ages of ages. Amen.
